title: The past tense of verbs with the vowel a
topic: the past tense of גָּר, קָם, בָּא
why: Short verbs like גָּר, קָם or בָּא have a very simple past tense: the vowel a stays and you add the endings from the previous lesson. With them, you can tell about your morning, from waking up to arriving at the office.

{"lessons": ["

Short verbs in the past

You know the short verbs with the vowel a in the present: גָּר (to live), קָם (to get up), רָץ (to run), בָּא (to come), שָׂם (to put). In the past, they're even simpler than כָּתַב: you keep the base and add the same endings (־תִּי, ־נוּ, ־תֶּם…).

קַמְתִּי בְּשֵׁשׁ.I got up at six. [kamti be-shesh]
גַּרְנוּ בְּחֵיפָה.We used to live in Haifa. [garnu be-Kheifa]

The trap: with הוּא and הִיא, the past is written just like the present! הוּא גָּר בְּחֵיפָה can mean \"he lives\" or \"he lived\" in Haifa. Context and time words (הַבֹּקֶר, קֹדֶם…) decide. With הֵם, there's no confusion: גָּרוּ (past), גָּרִים (present). In speech, stress helps too: in the past, הִיא קָמָה is stressed on \"ka,\" in the present on \"ma.\"

Before an ending that starts with a consonant, the kamats of the base becomes a patah: גָּר → גַּרְתִּי. Both are read a: you won't hear any difference.

As with כָּתַב, I and we are the same for a man and a woman: קַמְתִּי; you changes: קַמְתָּ [kamta] to a man, קַמְתְּ [kamt] to a woman.

בָּא: to come, with a silent א

PronounPastPronunciation
אֲנִיבָּאתִיbati
אַתָּהבָּאתָbata
אַתְּבָּאתbat
הוּאבָּאba
הִיאבָּאָהba'a
אֲנַחְנוּבָּאנוּbanu
אַתֶּםבָּאתֶםbatem
אַתֶּןבָּאתֶןbaten
הֵם / הֵןבָּאוּba'u

The א is still written but not pronounced, and the ת after it has no dot: בָּאתִי is simply read [bati]. Fun fact: בָּאת (you came, to a woman) sounds just like בַּת (daughter).

בָּאתִי לָעֲבוֹדָה בִּשְׁמוֹנֶה.I came to work at eight. [bati la-avoda bi-shmone]

Before a shva, בְּ becomes בִּ: you say בְּשֵׁשׁ [be-shesh], but בִּשְׁמוֹנֶה [bi-shmone].
